extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of lapidary science, natural philosophers, medieval gemologists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for assessing the qualities, virtues, and authenticity of gemstones (colour, hardness, transparency, medicinal/occult virtues, provenance, etc.) as presented in a medieval lapidary treatise. Covers physical identification tests, value indicators, and alleged therapeutic/magical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against lightning
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain stones (e.g., hyacinth) are said to render the wearer safe from lightning strikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses modes of application (carried, worn on a ring, kept under the tongue) and debates whether the effect is miraculous or natural. Several possible mechanisms are proposed (preventing the arrival of lightning, directing the mind of the person conducting business, or physically preventing the strike); the author notes skepticism and gives alternative explanations (e.g., fortune or natural causes). Examples and historical anecdotes (Zoroaster, Capaneus, Ajax) are mentioned as claims of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restores and strengthens spirits / relieves melancholy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some gems revive the spirits, cheer the heart, and counteract melancholy or excessive sadness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stones of a cold temperament are often said to be beneficial to human spirits by restoring or confirming vitality. The hyacinth is specifically credited with making the spirit pleasant and mild, aiding counsel, and increasing authority. The text links these virtues to temperament theory (humoral medicine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-inducing and divinatory properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain gems induce vivid dreams or assist divination when carried or placed appropriately (e.g., under the tongue, in rings, or on the body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author names several stones (amethyst, some emeralds, others) that move images in dreams and thus aid divination. Dryness, size, and specific colours/patterns affect a stone's propensity to produce dreams. Methods of excitation (association with other causes, or combination with certain substances) are discussed. Caution: the author notes that some claims are dubious or legendary and distinguishes between natural dream-induction and miraculous prophecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antidotal / alexipharmic (antipoison) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some gems (or bezoar-type substances) are credited with counteracting poisons or serving as antidotes to venom and other noxious substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'bezar' (bezoar) and certain named gems are said to neutralize venoms and protect against poisonous roots; sapphire is described as extinguishing anthrax in contact. The text records authoritative attributions but also warns of false reports; provenance and correct identification matter for medicinal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness / resistance to cutting, abrasion, and weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: A key property: how hard the gem is (capacity to resist fire, iron, and to cut or abrade other materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adamant (diamond) is given as the hardest (able to pierce iron), followed by other hard gems (sapphire, topaz, chrysolite). Hardness is linked to uses (weapon points, polish resistance). Tests and comparisons (resistance to fire, whether it can be filed or cut) are used as evidence. The text correlates hardness with value: generally the harder, the more valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lustre / brightness (nitorem, splendour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gem's surface shine, brilliance, and ability to reflect light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High splendour (as with diamond, sapphire, emerald) is prized and linked to value and some virtues (e.g., restoring sight or pleasing the eye). The author remarks that some stones have beauty but little virtue, so splendour alone does not guarantee medicinal effects. Polishing and exact smoothness of surface increase perceived splendour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour: hue, intensity, and purity
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific colour (hue), its intensity (diluted vs. deep), and purity are central to judging a gem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain colours are associated with optimal virtues (cerulean blue for sapphire, green for emerald). Diluted or vitiated colours reduce value and sometimes efficacy. Examples: amethyst (wine-colour) associated with temperance; hyacinth, carbuncle, chrysolite discussed by hue and supposed effects. Colour fastness and origin of colour (natural vs. exhalation/earth) are considered in authenticity assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / clarity (pellucidity / perspicuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a gem transmits or admits light—transparent, translucent, or opaque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent gems (crystal, fine sapphires, topazes) are often more valued; clarity affects splendour and some virtues. The text discusses how a gem can be partly translucent and partly opaque (creating bicoloured appearance) and how surface or internal properties cause this. Transparency is used as an identification marker and to infer quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific gravity / relative heaviness
rubrics_metrics.description: Heft (weight compared to glass or other materials) used to judge authenticity and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that certain gems (diamond, adamant) are heavier than glass and that gravity correlates with usefulness: heavier gems are often more useful and valuable. Glass and false stones tend to be lighter; weight is an indicator used alongside other tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Porosity and internal porosity-related vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of porosity (presence of pores/porous structure) which affects susceptibility to fire, liquids, and disintegration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porous gems allow fire to penetrate and hence are more easily damaged; porousness influences how a gem responds to heating and to oils or sweat. Porosity is also linked to whether a gem can be ground into powder or is friable. Tests: exposure to heat to observe damage; observing whether pores allow ingress of substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polishability / ability to take and retain a smooth finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the gem can be filed, polished, or retains a bright polish (file-touched vs. non-file-touched).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topaz/Chrysolite varieties that take the file/polish are noted as authentic in some usages. Polishing increases splendour; some gems lose brightness if too soft (overpolished) or if their substance is not suited. The text records whether a gem accepts a file as a sign of its material nature and commercial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brittleness / fragility (tendency to fracture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propensity to break or split under stress or heating rather than deforming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some gems (fragile emerald-like varieties) break easily when heated or struck. Brittleness affects use (e.g., in weapon tips or for long-term wear) and is contrasted with ductility of metals. Presence of tiny parts/pores increases fragility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat and moisture stability (reaction to sweat, heat, or sweat/heat causing loss of virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether exposure to heat, sweat, or continuous warmth degrades the gem's colour, shine, or supposed powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: opals and heliotropes lose powers with heat or sweat; some topaz varieties are durable whereas others from certain zones are softer. Stones found in humid or watery concretion zones behave differently. The text advises testing for heat sensitivity and notes that stability affects both medicinal efficacy and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic / humoral effects (which temperament or organ it aids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which bodily humours, temperaments, or organs the stone is said to benefit (e.g., heart, stomach, sight), and which diseases it addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed correspondences: sapphires and emeralds revive vision and help melancholics; some stones strengthen the heart or stomach; onyx tightens cold spirits and confirms strength. The author cites authorities (Galen, Albertus) and sometimes personal experiments, but also cautions on credulity. Use is tied to medieval humoral theory (hot/cold, dry/wet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream / imagination modulation by dryness and size
rubrics_metrics.description: A stone's dryness and size influence its ability to produce images in dreams or to affect imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drier stones and larger ones are said to move imagines in sleep more readily. The text observes that dryness is a sign for stones that induce dreams; examples and mechanisms (vapour, pores) are discussed. This criterion is linked to the dream-divination entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity, formation quality, and completeness (degree of development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a gem has reached full natural maturity (completeness of formation) — immature stones are common and inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfectly matured gems are rarer and more valuable; many stones are found immature and thus cheaper. The author notes that some gems never reach full maturity and that the stage of formation affects colour, hardness and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance / origin (locality of extraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographic origin of a gem (oriental vs others) affects perceived quality and price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly notes that eastern/oriental examples (e.g., oriental amethyst, topaz) are superior in some cases; particular localities yield superior specimens. Provenance is used as evidence for value and authenticity, though the author warns of false attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural surface figures / patterns and their significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of naturally occurring images or figures (animals, human faces, crosses, etc.) on or within the stone and whether such figures convey virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise distinguishes two kinds of figures: recurring/natural ones (which may have meaning) and accidental/fortuitous ones (which likely do not). It debates whether carved/painted images or natural figures give special powers, often concluding that most such claims are due to chance, fortune, or subsequent uses rather than a demonstrable natural virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystal habit / surface geometry (faceting, hexagonal habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The external geometric form of crystalline gems (e.g., hexagonal faces of crystal) as an identifying and natural property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author discusses why crystals have certain numbers of faces and relates surface geometry to natural generation rather than mystical causes. The crystal habit is an identification feature and is used to differentiate species (e.g., crystal vs. other gem types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction to acids / liquids (motion in vinegar or wine as diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stones (heliotrope, astrolite types) show motion or change in vinegar or wine; such reactions are used diagnostically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: certain stones move or 'stir' in vinegar/wine (a test for a fine/tenuous substance). The text treats these motions as an indication of the internal nature of the gem (vapourousness, lightness) and as a simple experiment readers can replicate to evaluate certain specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal attraction/repulsion and amuletic images (practical effects on creatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that some stones attract or repel animals (e.g., serpents) or when inscribed with images/figures confer special effects (e.g., Solomon's seal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: stones bearing serpent images purportedly attract serpents; some gems with Solomon's characters were allegedly found with special powers. The author debates whether these are natural properties of the stone, effects of fate, or the result of human action and warns that many reports are dubious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color patterning / internal veining and bands
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of veins, bands, or internal colour stratification (e.g., achates/agate banding) as diagnostic of species and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banding patterns (as in agate, onyx, sardonyx) are used to name varieties and to evaluate desirability; certain bandings (distinct or well-formed images) increase interest. The text gives examples of agate varieties bearing scenes or animal shapes and discusses whether such patterning is natural or caused by later processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency distribution across the stone (bicolour/partly translucent appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one part of a gem admits light and another does not, producing bi-coloured or variable appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains that differences in surface or internal permeability to light create such effects; these influence whether a gem appears black/dark in some parts and white/brilliant in others. This observation is used in identification and to explain why some gems show opposing colours or portions of translucence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency/rarity of type and scarcity-based value
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarity of a gem species or of specific perfect specimens strongly affects esteem and price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise notes some gems are rare in certain qualities (e.g., flawless chrysolite) and thus prized. Rarity is tied to maturity, locality, and the infrequency of particular patterns or colours; it is a major determinant of value independent of claimed virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of substance (absence of flaws, spots, or maculae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the gem is free from spots, stains, black veins or other visible defects which diminish splendour and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defects such as black maculae or internal impurities reduce brightness and are noted as grounds for lower valuation. Some defects also affect the purported virtues (e.g., a gem with defects less able to restore vision or resist heat). The text advises inspection for such flaws.
